solo.title: Solo 401(k)
solo.sub: Deferral plus an employer contribution, from the same profit
solo.body:
Room of $55,185 on your profit. Two halves, both funded by you; the plan just counts them separately.

LineAmountWhere it comes from
Your deferral, as the employee$24,500Capped at $24,500 at your age
Your contribution, as the employer$30,68520% of $153,425 of net self-employment earnings
Total into the account$55,185Both halves are you
Tax it removes$14,845Federal + California + self-employment, measured by running the engine twice
Your own spendable cash$40,340The real cost. Locked until 59½ without a penalty
Never computed as contribution × marginal rate — the rate falls as the deduction lowers income, and doing it the lazy way overstated this figure by $12,200 once.

Who it suits. Self-employed with no employees other than a spouse. That is the whole eligibility test.

The deadline that bites. The plan has to exist before you can fund it, and the employee and employer halves have different cut-offs.
solo.why: a.staff!=='none' ? 'You have staff \u2014 a Solo 401(k) is only for a practice with no employees other than a spouse.' : 'You said there is no spare profit \u2014 nothing to shelter.'

sep.title: SEP IRA
sep.sub: Employer-funded only, and openable after the year has ended
sep.body:
20% of $153,425 = $30,685. Less room than the Solo 401(k) because there is no employee half.

Its advantage is timing: it can be opened and funded right up to your filing deadline, extensions included — which makes it the usual choice once a year is already over.

Worth knowing. Hire anyone later and a SEP generally requires the same percentage for them as for you.
sep.why: 'You said there is no spare profit \u2014 nothing to shelter.'

assoc.title: Hiring associates changes which account you can use
assoc.sub: It does NOT force you to incorporate — but it does close the Solo 401(k)
assoc.body:
You do not need a corporation to employ an associate in California. The BBS requires a private practice to be “owned by a licensed health professional either independently or jointly with one or more other licensed health professionals” — independently means a sole owner, and no corporation is named anywhere in the requirement.

What the law does require is the employment relationship. Under BPC §4980.43.3 an associate “shall only perform mental health and related services as an employee or volunteer, and not as an independent contractor.” A sole proprietor can be that W-2 employer: EIN, payroll, EDD registration, workers’ compensation. Associates may only gain hours in private practice for the first six years after registration.

What hiring changesEffect
What it does not change
Your entityA sole proprietor can employ staff. No corporation required.
What it does change, and this is the expensive part
Solo 401(k)Closes. One non-excludable common-law employee and it stops being a one-participant plan.
Who is excludableUnder 21 · under 1,000 hours in a year · under 500 hours in each of two consecutive years · non-resident aliens. A part-time associate may well be excludable; a full-time one is not.
SEP IRAGenerally requires the same percentage for eligible employees. Cheap alone, expensive with staff.
SIMPLE IRABuilt for exactly this: deferral plus a mandatory 3% match.
The corporation questionGets cheaper, not more necessary — you are running payroll either way, so the payroll-service cost stops being an argument against incorporating.
This is the one place where the two decisions on this page genuinely interact.

So the honest answer: hiring associates does not make you incorporate. It closes your best deferral account and quietly removes one of the reasons not to incorporate. Those are different things, and most write-ups conflate them.
assoc.why: 'Only bites once someone else is on your payroll.'

simple.title: SIMPLE IRA
simple.sub: Deferral plus a mandatory 3% match, built for small teams
simple.body:
$22,703 of room: $18,100 deferral plus a mandatory 3% of $153,425. A solo practice always qualifies for the higher small-employer limit.

Cannot be run in the same year as a Solo 401(k). That is a rule, not a preference — picking one closes the other.

Must be set up earlier in the year than the others, and money out within the first two years carries a steeper penalty than a normal early withdrawal.
simple.why: a.spare==='none' ? 'No spare profit to shelter.' : 'With no employees, the Solo 401(k) gives more room at the same effort, and nothing forces you into a SIMPLE.'

ira.title: Traditional IRA
ira.sub: Allowed, but not deductible at your income
ira.body: Annual limit $7,500 at your age. Deductible share: $0. A non-deductible contribution is still permitted, and it is the one account here not tied to self-employment, so it works alongside any of the others.
ira.why: 'Fully phased out at ' + m(N.profit) + ' of profit once you have a plan of your own \u2014 the contribution is allowed, the deduction is not.'

corp.title: Professional corporation
corp.sub: S-corp election, a defensible salary, payroll every fortnight
corp.body:

corp.why: 'You would rather keep it simple \u2014 and on your numbers it is worth ' + m(N.scorpNet) + ' a year, so simple is also the cheaper answer.'

llc.title: LLC
llc.sub: Not a choice for a California-licensed therapist
llc.body: A California-licensed MFT, LCSW, LPCC or psychologist cannot form an LLC to provide licensed services — Cal. Corp. Code §17701.04(e). The real choice is sole proprietorship or a California professional corporation (for MFTs, a Marriage and Family Therapy Corporation, 51%+ MFT-owned per §13401.5) which can then elect S-corp treatment federally.
llc.why: 'Blocked by statute for anyone on this page, whatever the answers.'

salary.title: The salary split
salary.sub: How much of the profit is wage, and how much is distribution
salary.body:
The whole election turns on this number. Too high and there is nothing left to distribute; too low and it is the arrangement the IRS actually challenges.

SalaryShare of profitPayroll taxRisk
$50,00031%lowerAggressive — hard to defend
$80,00050%moderateThe usual starting benchmark
$100,00063%higherComfortable, and cheaper to justify
The 50%-of-profit convention is a private-practice folk rule, not an IRS threshold. See the reasonable-compensation block.
salary.why: 'Only a question once you have a corporation to pay a salary out of.'

wage.title: What a defensible salary looks like
wage.sub: BLS metro wages and what California therapy S-corps actually run through payroll
wage.body:
Two independent anchors, neither of which is a rule.

SourceFigureWhat it is
BLS OEWS, CA MFTs$61,450–$98,400Metro mean wages, May 2023, SOC 21-1013
Census CBP, CA NAICS 621330$59,243Payroll per employee at S-corp establishments with 1–4 employees
Your salary$80,000135% of the peer figure
Employment is a 12 March point-in-time count while payroll is full-year, so part-year staff drag the per-employee figure down. Evidence of what peers do, not a target and not a safe harbour.
wage.why: 'Only matters once you are setting a salary.'

setup.title: What incorporating actually involves
setup.sub: Five filings to start, then two returns and 26 payroll runs a year
setup.body:
1. Articles of Incorporation — filed with the CA Secretary of State, as a professional corporation.
  2. Bylaws and share issuance — 51%+ MFT-owned per §13401.5.
  3. EIN — from the IRS, before payroll can exist.
  4. Form 2553 — the S-corp election itself. Deadline-sensitive.
  5. EDD registration — California payroll tax account.

Then, every year: Form 1120-S and CA Form 100S by 15 March, W-2s by 31 January, a Statement of Information, and the franchise tax.

Naming is governed by B&P Code §4987.7. BBS registration of the corporation is not required, per Corp Code §13401(b).
setup.why: 'Nothing to file if you stay a sole proprietor.'

ss.title: Social Security
ss.sub: What a salary below your profit costs, decades out
ss.body:
On the sole-proprietor path every dollar of profit is credited earnings. A salary below your profit credits less, for every year you do it.

Claim atSole proprietorProfessional corpWhy
62$2,787/mo$2,239/mo×0.70 of PIA
67$3,981/mo$3,199/mofull retirement age
70$4,936/mo$3,967/mo×1.24 of PIA
The 62 and 70 rows are the 67 figure scaled by the published factors. Bend points lock at 62, so any projection made now is an approximation and is labelled as one.

Abroad: Germany, Portugal, France and Australia have totalization agreements. The UAE does not. Cuba and North Korea are blocked. Medicare does not travel.
ss.why: 'Decades away, and you are not taking a salary below your profit \u2014 nothing here changes for you yet.'

compound.title: What one year becomes
compound.sub: This year's contribution, left alone until 67
compound.body: One year of $55,185, at 11% for the 27 years to 67. Nothing else in this chapter compounds — the structure decision is worth its face value every year and no more.

prevalence.title: What California therapists actually do
prevalence.body:
Nobody surveys this. The Census does publish it, derived from tax filings rather than a questionnaire.

UniverseSole propS corpOthern
All CA mental-health practices78%18%4%33,660
Practices large enough to run payroll11%72%17%6,953
The inversion is the point: a sole proprietor has no payroll and lands in the nonemployer file; a corporation paying its owner a W-2 has payroll by definition. The two universes are near mutually exclusive on exactly the axis being measured.

1,049 California S corporations in this category run zero payroll — shareholders taking distributions and paying themselves no salary at all. That is the reasonable-compensation exposure this chapter warns about, as a counted number rather than a hypothetical. Average receipts $89,112, against $60,563 for sole proprietors.

NAICS 621330 covers all non-physician mental-health practitioners with no licence-level cut, and counts establishments rather than therapists.

experts.title: What the lawyers and accountants say
experts.sub: Three named sources who disagree about the threshold
experts.body:
Michael J. Leonard, Esq. (San Diego Corporate Law) comes down firmly on the corporation, calling it “the California business entity of choice for marriage and family therapists”.

Heard, an accounting firm working only with therapists, sets a floor rather than a rule: $100,000 of annual net income before the election is worth making, and puts the running cost at roughly $4,400 a year.

The IRS publishes no percentage and never has. The requirement is that an officer performing more than minor services be paid reasonable compensation for work actually done, before any distribution. The “50% of profit” figure repeated across every private-practice blog is convention, not law.

setax.title: How self-employment tax actually works
setax.sub: The mechanic the whole chapter turns on
setax.body:
Self-employment tax is Social Security and Medicare for people with no employer to split it with, so you pay both halves — 12.4% + 2.9%.

StepOn your numbers
Net profit$158,849
× 92.35%$153,425 — the SE base
Social Security, 12.4%up to the $184,500 wage base
Medicare, 2.9%no cap; +0.9% above $200,000 single / $250,000 joint
Half of what you pay is deductible against income tax, which is why no lever here is worth its headline rate.

The S-corp election works by moving part of your profit out of that base and into a distribution. That is the entire mechanism — and the reason a salary that is too low is the thing that gets challenged.

audit.title: Audit risk, honestly
audit.sub: What actually gets challenged, and what does not
audit.body:
The challenged arrangement is almost never “you incorporated”. It is “you took $150,000 of distributions and paid yourself $20,000”.

The defence is a file, made before anyone asks: what you do, what comparable clinicians earn, how many hours are clinical versus management, and why the number you picked follows from that. Nu-Look Design v. Commissioner, 356 F.3d 290 (3d Cir. 2004) is the usual citation for recharacterisation.

Keep the payroll discipline: run it on a schedule, file the W-2, and never take a distribution in a year with no salary in it.
audit.why: 'A sole proprietor has no reasonable-compensation exposure to manage.'
